client: I've been really struggling since my dog passed away last month. It's like all the little things that used to make me happy just... don't anymore. I go through my day feeling kind of hollow, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything.
therapist: Losing your dog is a real and profound grief — the hollow feeling you're describing makes complete sense, because that daily companionship and joy leaves such a significant gap in your life. I also hear your doubt about whether talking will help, and I want you to know that skepticism is completely valid, not something you need to push past. I'm curious — when you imagine what "feeling better" might even look like right now, what comes to mind, if anything?

client: I guess... feeling better would just mean not waking up and automatically reaching for him before I remember he's gone. That moment every morning is the worst part — it's like losing him all over again, every single day. I don't know if talking can change that, honestly, because it's not a thought problem, it's just... he's not there.
therapist: That moment you're describing — reaching for him before memory catches up — is one of the most tender and painful parts of grief, and you're right that it isn't just a "thought problem" to be solved. What you're experiencing is your love for him, still looking for somewhere to land each morning. I wonder, in those moments after the wave hits, is there anything — even something small and imperfect — that has ever helped you get through the next few minutes of the day?

client: I appreciate you saying that — that it's my love still looking for somewhere to land. That actually made me tear up a little, because it feels true in a way I couldn't put into words myself. As for what helps in those next few minutes... honestly, sometimes I just lie there and let it hurt, because getting up feels like I'm leaving him behind all over again.
therapist: It means a lot that those words resonated, and those tears are a sign of how real and deep this bond was — there's nothing to push away there. I also want to gently reflect something back to you: staying in that moment to honor the pain makes sense, and yet I'm wondering if part of you also worries that moving through the day means moving *away* from him. What do you think it would mean about your love for him if you did get up?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Because yeah, I think that's exactly it — like if I get up and make coffee and go through my day, it feels like I'm saying he didn't matter, or that I'm okay with him being gone. And I'm not okay with it, not even a little bit.
therapist: What you've just uncovered is so important — you've been using your pain as a way of staying loyal to him, which is a beautiful impulse even as it's keeping you stuck in that bed each morning. But I want to offer a gentle alternative thought: what if making your coffee and carrying him *with you* through the day is actually a deeper form of love than staying still in the hurt? I'm curious — are there moments in your day, even brief ones, where you feel his presence or influence in a way that feels like connection rather than loss?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it also feels a little too neat, you know? Like, if I just make my coffee and "carry him with me," am I not just pretending everything is okay when it's really not? As for moments of connection rather than loss... honestly, most of the time when I think of him, it just hurts, but maybe sometimes when I hear a certain song he used to play, there's something there that's not quite so sharp.
therapist: Your pushback is really important and I don't want to gloss over it — you're right that "carrying him with you" can't just be a tidy reframe that papers over real pain, and your instinct to resist that is healthy, not resistant. But I'm struck by what you said about that song — that there's "something there that's not quite so sharp," because that sounds less like pretending and more like a genuine moment where love and memory coexist without being purely agony. I'm wondering, when that song comes on, what is it that feels different in that moment compared to the mornings?

client: I think... when the song comes on, I'm not trying to do anything. Like, in the mornings I wake up and immediately there's this weight, this awareness that he's gone, and I'm sort of bracing against it. But with the song, I'm not fighting anything, I'm just kind of... in it, and somehow that's easier to bear.
therapist: You've just noticed something really profound about yourself — that bracing against the pain actually intensifies it, while simply being *in* the moment with him, without trying to manage it, creates a little more room to breathe. That's not a small insight, and it came entirely from you. I'm curious whether there might be a way to bring even a little of that "not fighting" quality into those morning moments — not to make them hurt less, but just to hold them differently?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to try that... but mornings are when I'm most raw, before I've had any time to build up any kind of armor for the day. It's like you're asking me to be open and undefended at exactly the moment when I feel most vulnerable, and I'm not sure I have the capacity for that when I'm half-asleep and he's already gone to school without saying goodbye. What if I just fall apart completely instead of finding that breathing room you're describing?
therapist: I notice you mentioned him going to school — it sounds like grief may be touching more than just your dog right now, and I want to make sure I'm understanding your world fully. And your fear of falling apart completely in that vulnerable morning moment is so valid — I'd never want to suggest you simply lower your defenses when you're already at your most exposed. I'm wondering, what does "falling apart completely" look like in your mind — is it something that has happened before, and if so, what actually got you through it?

client: Yeah, falling apart completely... I guess it means like, I just can't stop crying and I can't function, I can't get myself to work or even just make a cup of coffee. It has happened before, actually, when my dad left when I was a teenager — I basically shut down for weeks and my mom had to kind of drag me back to life. I got through it because she was there, but now she's far away and my son is leaving and my dog is gone, and I just... I don't have that same safety net anymore, and that's what scares me the most.
therapist: What you've just shared helps me understand so much more — this grief over your dog is also touching something much older and deeper, this fear of being left without a safety net at exactly the moment you need one most. And I want to gently reflect that you *did* get through that devastating time as a teenager, even when it felt impossible, which tells me something real about your capacity to survive loss even when it's this hard. I'm wondering — as your son prepares to leave and you're facing all of this at once, is there anyone in your life right now, even imperfectly, who could offer even a small piece of what your mom once did for you?

client: I appreciate what you're saying about getting through things before, but honestly, it doesn't feel like proof that I can do it again — it just feels like I got lucky, or I was younger and more resilient somehow. As for people in my life right now... I mean, there are a few, but it's complicated. My friend Diane checks in sometimes, but I always feel like I'm too much for her, like if I really unloaded everything I'm carrying she'd pull back.
therapist: That belief — that you're "too much" — is worth pausing on, because it's doing something important: it's keeping you isolated at exactly the moment you most need connection, and I wonder where that idea first took root for you. And I want to gently push back on the "luck" explanation too, because luck doesn't drag itself through weeks of shutdown and come out the other side — that was *you*, even if it didn't feel like strength at the time. I'm curious — has Diane ever actually pulled back when you've shared something hard, or is that something you're anticipating based on a fear rather than something she's shown you?

client: Honestly, when I think about it... Diane hasn't actually pulled away when things got hard. There was that one time I mentioned feeling overwhelmed at work and she just listened, didn't make it weird or anything. But I keep waiting for the moment she decides it's too much, like I'm just anticipating some eventual rejection that hasn't happened yet.
therapist: What you just did there is really significant — you examined the evidence and found that the story you've been telling yourself about Diane doesn't actually match her behavior, which takes real honesty and courage to see. That anticipation of eventual rejection sounds like it might have a longer history than just Diane — like maybe it's a pattern that makes sense given what you've experienced with loss and people leaving. I'm wondering, what do you think it would feel like to let Diane in just a little more than usual, not everything at once, but just one small, honest moment — and what's the worst you'd actually expect to happen?
